keyVerseText: And last of all he was seen of me also, as of one born out of due time. one: or, an abortive
rootMeaning: The word ἔκτρωμα (éktrōma) derives from the Greek preposition ἐκ (ek), meaning 'out of' or 'from,' combined with τιτρώσκω (titrōskō), which means 'to wound.' This etymology conveys the sense of something 'wounded out' or 'born out of due time,' emphasizing a birth that is untimely and marked by injury or imperfection. This root meaning deepens the common English gloss of 'born out of due time' by highlighting the unnatural or premature nature of the event, suggesting a disruption in the normal process of life.
usageInScripture: The term ἔκτρωμα appears only once in the New Testament, specifically in 1 Corinthians 15:8, where it is translated as 'of one born out of due time' or 'an abortive.' Its singular occurrence limits the range of its usage, but the consistent translation underscores its meaning related to untimely or premature birth. The lexicon notes its use in the Septuagint to describe miscarriages or aborted births, reinforcing its connotation of something incomplete or prematurely ended.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ἔκτρωμα as an 'untimely birth' or miscarriage enriches our grasp of human brokenness and imperfection in the biblical narrative. It reminds believers of the frailty of life and the reality of suffering even from the earliest stages of existence. In the Christian faith, this concept can metaphorically reflect the experience of being 'born out of due time' in one's spiritual journey, highlighting God's grace in redeeming what is prematurely or imperfectly formed. It also points to the significance of Christ's resurrection as the perfect, timely fulfillment of God's redemptive plan, contrasting with the idea of an abortive or incomplete event.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Corinthians 15:8, Paul describes himself as 'one born out of due time,' using ἔκτρωμα to express his sense of being an unexpected or untimely witness to the risen Christ. This word choice conveys a sense of being set apart or coming into the faith under unusual circumstances, emphasizing God's sovereign grace in Paul's call. The term enriches the verse by portraying Paul’s ministry as something that, though seemingly premature or surprising, is fully embraced and used by God for His purposes.
